title.en: Curl and circulation around a loop

summary: Compare a local curl component with circulation per unit area, distinguishing the finite-disk average from its shrinking-disk limit.
objective: Build a field where I can move and tilt a small loop, read its circulation and compare it with the curl component along the loop normal.
intent_signals: Show what curl measures at a point.
Compare a circulation integral with the curl of the field.
example_prompts: Build a curl demonstration with a movable oriented loop and a circulation readout.
Show a field whose curl is zero and a field where it is not.
negative_signals: Not a fluid dynamics simulation; no velocity boundary conditions or viscosity.
Not a proof of Stokes theorem: agreement in the scene is numerical, within a stated tolerance.
not_for: Not a fluid dynamics simulation; no velocity boundary conditions or viscosity.
Not a proof of Stokes theorem: agreement in the scene is numerical, within a stated tolerance.

entities.name: Field and probe point
entities.guidance: Show the analytic field sparsely plus a highlighted probe point whose curl vector is drawn with a declared display scale.

entities.name: Oriented loop
entities.guidance: Give the loop a visible traversal direction and a right-hand normal, since circulation changes sign with orientation.

entities.name: Numerical readout
entities.guidance: Display the loop circulation, the loop area, their ratio and the curl component along the normal, so the comparison is explicit.

state_contract.model: A prescribed smooth analytic field, a loop with centre, positive radius and normal whose spanning disk lies inside the smooth domain, a numerically quadratured circulation, and the analytic curl at the centre. Circulation divided by area is the average of the normal curl component over the disk; it equals the centre value only in the shrinking-loop limit, or exactly when the field has constant curl.
state_contract.authority: The analytic field is authoritative; both the circulation estimate and the curl vector are derived from it, so no readout may be authored independently.
actions: Move the loop through the field.
Shrink the loop radius and watch the ratio converge.
Switch to a field with zero curl and reset.

invariants: Reversing the loop traversal reverses the sign of the circulation and of the reported normal.

Alignment and perpendicularity statements hold in the shrinking-loop limit, or exactly for a declared constant-curl field. For a varying field a finite loop whose normal is perpendicular to the centre curl can still have nonzero circulation, so the scene reports the ratio as a disk average, not as the centre value.
For a conservative field the circulation stays within the stated tolerance of zero for every loop position and orientation.

For smooth fields the exact disk average tends to the centre curl component as radius tends to zero, without requiring monotonic improvement at successive radii. Quadrature error and floating-point cancellation can limit the computed comparison; distinguish them from finite-radius averaging and report radius and sample count.
motion_guidance: Animate a marker travelling the loop in the declared direction so the sign convention is visible, not implied.
Shrink the loop smoothly and show the computed ratio alongside the analytic component, preserving nonmonotonic changes and numerical limits instead of forcing visual convergence.
known_limits: Circulation is computed by quadrature on a discretised loop; its accuracy depends on the sample count.
Only smooth prescribed fields are handled; singular fields need their own treatment.

For a field with varying curl the finite-loop ratio differs from the centre value; for example a field whose curl has a component growing with position gives nonzero circulation on a loop whose normal is perpendicular to the centre curl.
Authored guidance only: no scene runtime, rendering or numerical calibration has been run for this recipe.

claims.statement: For a differentiable vector field the curl is a vector that measures the tendency of particles near a point to rotate about the axis pointing in its direction, which is the sense of the paddlewheel interpretation.
claims.scope: Definition and interpretation as cited; the loop comparison in the scene is a numerical illustration.

claims.statement: If a field is conservative then its curl is zero, and on a simply connected domain a field with zero curl is conservative.
claims.scope: Domain condition matters: the converse requires simple connectedness as cited.

claims.statement: Stokes' theorem equates the circulation of a field around a positively oriented simple closed boundary curve with the flux of its curl through a compatible piecewise smooth oriented surface, for fields with continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing the surface, and the normal component of curl at a point is the limit of circulation divided by area over shrinking disks.
claims.scope: Smooth fields and compatible oriented surfaces as cited; the finite-radius ratio in the scene is an area average that tends to the centre value by continuity, not an identity at finite radius.

object_craft.structure: A torus ring with an arrowhead on the ring itself plus a normal rod, so orientation is legible from any camera angle.
object_craft.material: Single accent for the loop with a matching but lighter value for its normal; the field arrows stay neutral.
object_craft.articulation: The ring rotates about its centre under the normal control and rebuilds sample points when the radius changes.

object_craft.structure: Sparse arrows plus a distinctly larger curl arrow at the probe with its own scale legend.
object_craft.material: The curl arrow uses a reserved accent that appears nowhere else, since it is the quantity under study.
object_craft.articulation: Recomputed analytically whenever the probe moves.

physical_contract.scope: Quadrature of a line integral over a prescribed field; no fluid or particle simulation.
checks: Compare the computed ratio with the centre normal curl component across declared positive radii, accounting separately for quadrature error and finite-radius averaging. The smooth-field limit does not require every radius reduction to improve agreement.
Reversing traversal flips the sign of the reported circulation.
